ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (epilepsy) Consultation — Florence Griffith Joyner — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: EEG and MRI results: focal epilepsy from a left orbitofrontal cavernous malformation; epilepsy consultation, levetiracetam with folic acid, and neurosurgical opinion requested

text.paragraph: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure on a flight two and a half weeks ago in a 36-year-old former Olympic sprinter who still trains daily, with treatment for seizures elsewhere in the past (records requested) and no antiseizure medication now. EEG and MRI of the brain with susceptibility-weighted imaging are booked this week. Please see her within two weeks to interpret them, decide whether this is epilepsy, and advise on treatment and safety. [S]

list.item: Is this epilepsy, and what do the EEG and MRI show about its cause?
Which antiseizure medication do you recommend for a woman who could become pregnant, and what counseling should go with it?
If the MRI shows a structural lesion, such as a vascular malformation, scar or tumor, should she see neurosurgery about removing it?
What should she be told about SUDEP, nocturnal monitoring, and safety with water, heights and sleep?
When can she return to sprint training, flying and driving?

text.paragraph: Ms. Griffith Joyner, 36, is seen at the request of Dr. Vanterpool two weeks after her first visit for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on a flight. Others described stiffening and then jerking of all four limbs with confusion afterwards; she remembers nothing of it. She has had treatment for seizures elsewhere in the past, and those records have not arrived. There was no provoking factor. She has had no seizure since. She trains most days, flies often for work, and has stopped driving. She is not pregnant and is not planning a pregnancy now. She wants the details kept private. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Florence Griffith was born in Los Angeles on December 21, 1959, the seventh of eleven children, and grew up from the age of four in a public housing project in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles. Reference works give her given names in both orders, Delorez Florence and Florence Delorez. [D]

She ran for California State University, Northridge, and then for UCLA, graduating in 1983, and won the silver medal in the 200 meters at the 1984 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, competing as Florence Griffith. [D]

In 1988 she set a world record of 10.49 seconds for 100 meters at the U.S. Olympic Trials and, at the Seoul Olympic Games, won gold medals in the 100 meters, the 200 meters (in a world record of 21.34 seconds) and the 4 x 100 meters relay, and a silver medal in the 4 x 400 meters relay. She retired from competition in 1989. [D]

In 1993 she was appointed co-chair of the President's Council on Physical Fitness and Sports, and in 1995 she was inducted into the U.S. Track and Field Hall of Fame. She also worked as a designer of clothing and athletic wear. [D]
In April 1996 she had a seizure on an airplane on the way to St. Louis. She was taken to hospital and discharged the next day, and her family asked that no other details be released. [D]
Coroner's investigation records, reported after her death, state that she had a generalized (grand mal) seizure in 1990 and had been treated for seizures in 1990, 1993 and 1994. [D]

list.item: Focal epilepsy with structural cause (G40.209). The seizure was focal in onset, from the left orbitofrontal cortex, and spread to both hemispheres (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic). The EEG discharges match the site of the cavernous malformation. Under the ILAE 1984 practical definition, one unprovoked seizure with an epileptogenic lesion and matching discharges is epilepsy, because the risk of another seizure exceeds 60%; her earlier seizures add to that. I recommend starting an antiseizure medication now. For a woman who could become pregnant, levetiracetam or lamotrigine carries the lowest risk of birth defects; levetiracetam reaches an effective dose at once and does not interact with hormonal contraception, while lamotrigine needs about six weeks of titration and its level falls with estrogen. Valproate should be avoided. Levetiracetam can cause irritability or low mood, which should be asked about at each visit. She should take folic acid 0.4 mg daily and plan any pregnancy with the epilepsy team. SUDEP should be discussed with her at diagnosis; today's visit did not allow a full discussion, so I have asked that it be the first item at her next primary care visit: SUDEP is uncommon but real, tonic-clonic seizures are the main risk, and freedom from them is the best protection. [S]

Solitary cerebral cavernous malformation, left orbitofrontal (Q28.3). A single cavernous malformation with a developmental venous anomaly is the sporadic form, so familial genetic testing is not needed. Because it is the source of her epilepsy and lies in accessible cortex, neurosurgical evaluation is recommended: complete removal with the surrounding hemosiderin rim gives a high chance of freedom from seizures, and early surgery is associated with better seizure outcomes than surgery after years of seizures. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Vanterpool's intake note and laboratory results: blood count, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, creatinine, ALT and creatine kinase normal; pregnancy test negative. Sleep-deprived EEG: intermittent left frontal sharp waves and focal slowing, maximal at F7 and Fp1; no generalized discharges. MRI of the brain, epilepsy protocol with susceptibility-weighted imaging and gadolinium: a 1.4 cm cavernous malformation in the left orbitofrontal cortex with a complete hemosiderin rim (Zabramski type II), an adjacent developmental venous anomaly, no other lesion, and no acute hemorrhage. [S]

list.item: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily from today, with mood and irritability checked at each visit; switch to lamotrigine if mood effects are troublesome; avoid valproate. [S]
Folic acid 0.4 mg daily; contraception and pregnancy planning reviewed at each visit. [S]
Neurosurgical evaluation within three weeks for lesionectomy of the cavernous malformation with its hemosiderin rim; continue levetiracetam through and for at least two years after surgery. [S]
Seizure diary, written seizure action plan, and emergency services for a seizure lasting five minutes or more. [S]
SUDEP counseling as the first item at the next primary care visit, with nocturnal supervision or a wrist-worn seizure detection device. [S]
Safety: showers instead of baths, swimming only with a companion who knows first aid, no heights or working alone near water; flying is allowed with medication in hand luggage. [S]
Driving only when the California DMV clears her after review of her seizure control; return to training on a graded plan after any surgery. [S]
Report sudden severe headache or new neurological symptoms at once, which could mean bleeding from the malformation. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Vanterpool, who saw her the same day. The EEG and MRI images were shown and explained to Ms. Griffith Joyner, who chose to start levetiracetam today and to meet the neurosurgeon; she decides who else receives this note. [S]
Follow-up: Epilepsy review after the neurosurgical opinion and again after any surgery; Dr. Vanterpool continues primary care and shares the monitoring. [S]
